title: Jeremiah 51:1–14
context: The LORD continues against Babylon and Lebkamai (51:1), a name many interpreters take as a coded way of writing “Chaldea”; that explanation is held with caution. His people are called again to flee (51:6). Babylon, once a golden cup in the LORD’s hand (51:7), has suddenly fallen (51:8). The LORD has stirred up the kings of the Medes (51:11) and sworn by himself to fill Babylon with enemies (51:14).

verses.text: The LORD says: “Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against those who dwell in Lebkamai, a destroying wind.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against those who dwell in Lebkamai, a destroying wind.” Arminian readers see God sending judgment like a wind on Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD raising up the destroyer. Many interpreters take “Lebkamai” as a coded name for the Chaldeans, though readers in this tradition hold that explanation with caution.

verses.text: I will send to Babylon strangers, who will winnow her. They will empty her land; for in the day of trouble they will be against her all around.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will send to Babylon strangers, who will winnow her.” Arminian readers see the image of winnowing: Babylon scattered like chaff by foreign invaders under God’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the winnowing image. Babylon, which scattered nations, is now scattered, and readers in this tradition see the reversal as evidence of God’s just rule.

verses.text: Against him who bends, let the archer bend his bow, also against him who lifts himself up in his coat of mail. Don’t spare her young men! Utterly destroy all her army!
verses.arminianNotes: “Against him who bends, let the archer bend his bow.” Arminian readers see a battle command urging that Babylon’s army be given no reprieve, read soberly as war poetry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the decisive defeat of Babylon’s forces announced. The harsh language reflects ancient warfare, and readers in this tradition read it as judgment poetry rather than as a general model for conduct.

verses.text: They will fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and thrust through in her streets.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and thrust through in her streets.” Arminian readers see the battle reaching into Babylon’s own streets, as it once reached Jerusalem’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of Jerusalem’s fate. Readers in this tradition read the verse soberly and do not take pleasure in the suffering it describes.

verses.text: For Israel is not forsaken, nor Judah, by his God, by the LORD of Armies; though their land is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “For Israel is not forsaken, nor Judah, by his God … though their land is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.” Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to a guilty people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant faithfulness that persists despite guilt. Readers in both traditions commonly hear grace here: the LORD does not abandon his people even when their sin is great.

verses.text: “Flee out of the middle of Babylon! Everyone save his own life! Don’t be cut off in her iniquity, for it is the time of the LORD’s vengeance. He will give to her a recompense.
verses.arminianNotes: “Flee out of the middle of Babylon! Everyone save his own life!” Arminian readers see an urgent call to escape judgment and not share in Babylon’s iniquity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the summons to separate from the doomed city. Some readers note that Revelation 18:4 takes up a similar call, cited here by reference, and readers in this tradition hold that link as a later reuse.

verses.text: Babylon has been a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, who made all the earth drunk. The nations have drunk of her wine; therefore the nations have gone mad.
verses.arminianNotes: “Babylon has been a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, who made all the earth drunk.” Arminian readers see Babylon as the instrument of God’s wrath, echoing the cup of 25:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Babylon as the cup in the LORD’s hand. The existing Judges 9:23 box covers God using agents who are then judged; this note points there rather than restating it.

verses.text: Babylon has suddenly fallen and been destroyed! Wail for her! Take balm for her pain. Perhaps she may be healed.
verses.arminianNotes: “Babylon has suddenly fallen and been destroyed! Wail for her!” Arminian readers see a sudden fall and an ironic call for healing that cannot help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Babylon’s sudden collapse. Revelation 18:2 echoes the cry of Babylon’s fall, as does Isaiah 21:9, both cited by reference; readers in this tradition note those echoes without merging the passages.

verses.text: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed. Forsake her, and let’s each go into his own country; for her judgment reaches to heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies.
verses.arminianNotes: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed.” Arminian readers see those who tried to help Babylon abandoning the effort, since its judgment “reaches to heaven.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the futility of attempts to heal Babylon. Who speaks here is not specified, perhaps foreigners in the city, and readers in this tradition hold the identification loosely.

verses.text: ‘The LORD has produced our righteousness. Come, and let’s declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God.’
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD has produced our righteousness. Come, and let’s declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God.” Arminian readers hear God’s people praising him for vindicating them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD vindicating his people. The phrase “our righteousness” here likely means vindication or the setting right of their cause, and readers in this tradition hear joyful praise for God’s work.

verses.text: “Make the arrows sharp! Hold the shields firmly! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose is against Babylon, to destroy it; for it is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance of his temple.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes.” Arminian readers see God moving rulers to carry out his purpose against Babylon, while the Medes pursue their own aims.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD stirring kings to fulfill his purpose. Readers can consult the existing Isaiah 13:17 box on the Medes rather than a new discussion here.

verses.text: Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon! Make the watch strong! Set the watchmen, and prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both purposed and done that which he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: “Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon! Make the watch strong!” Arminian readers hear ironic commands: Babylon may prepare its defenses, but the LORD has purposed and done what he said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the certainty of the LORD’s purpose. Readers in this tradition note that both the purposing and the doing are ascribed to the LORD, stressing his faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: You who dwell on many waters, abundant in treasures, your end has come, the measure of your covetousness.
verses.arminianNotes: “You who dwell on many waters, abundant in treasures, your end has come.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s wealth and waterways unable to secure its future.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the end of Babylon’s greed. The phrase “the measure of your covetousness” suggests that its time has run out, and readers in this tradition see God setting limits to human ambition.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies has sworn by himself, saying, ‘Surely I will fill you with men, as with locusts, and they will lift up a shout against you.’
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD of Armies has sworn by himself.” Arminian readers see the certainty of judgment guaranteed by God’s own oath, since there is no greater name to swear by.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s oath as an unshakable guarantee. Readers in this tradition commonly connect oaths by himself with passages such as Hebrews 6:13, cited by reference, which stress God’s faithfulness.
